exactOriginalMemberTasksAndGuards.task: Identify tumor at a cut inked edge versus a close negative edge and a separately submitted final margin.
exactOriginalMemberTasksAndGuards.gap: The reporting table is strong but physical specimen geometry is the hard idea. A simple oriented-tissue cutaway with main edge, additional tissue and final outer edge would explain why the original edge need not remain final, while a second inset distinguishes distance from tumor at ink.
guardrails: No automatic operation or universal adequate-distance rule.
Ink artifacts and unresolved orientation cannot be erased by a tidy sketch.
Do not depict a local negative edge as whole-body clearance.

sourceDepth: Same existing selected CAP/FDA/NCI/CONSORT passages and archived primary abstracts; no new access/science/clinical claim

readerCopy.title: Which edge is final?
readerCopy.alt: Panel 1 of 2. Fictional tissue schematics show invasive cells at the original lateral ink of a main specimen and at the final outer ink of a separate, confirmed lateral strip. An orientation inset keeps the specimens separate, with the old-facing surface distinct from the final outer edge. Continue to panel 2 for DCIS near versus at ink.
readerCopy.caption: Panel 1 of 2: relate the main and additional specimens before naming the final edge. Continue below for DCIS near or at ink.

acceptedOverallCaption: A final margin depends on the related specimens and their orientation. A small gap from ink is different from cancer at ink; adequacy still needs clinical context.
